name: arrange-act-assert
intent: Structure a behaviour-focused test as an explicit arrange phase that establishes only its preconditions, one act interaction with the system under test, and an assert phase that checks the resulting observable outcome, so a failure localises to one behaviour without pretending that the runner enforces sequencing.
problem: A test that hides fixture work in hooks, interleaves several actions and assertions, or treats Arrange/Act/Assert labels as enforcement becomes a small workflow that is hard to read and hard to diagnose: the reader cannot tell which state is intentional, which call is under test, or which outcome failed.
context: Any behaviour-focused automated test - xUnit-style class, spec/BDD runner or plain test function - where the test method is the unit of documentation. The pattern matters most when tests outlive their authors (legacy code, shared libraries, contract suites), when fixtures differ per test or are expensive enough to share, and when the suite is used to learn what a system does.
benefits: A failure localises: because exactly one act beat runs, the failing assertion points at the behaviour the test exercises instead of at some line in a mixed block.
The test reads as documentation: arrange, act and assert are visible at a glance (as comments, blocks or macros), so preconditions, behaviour and expectation can be reviewed separately.
Refactoring and review get cheaper: a missing, duplicated or interleaved beat is obvious, which turns 'this test is too long' into a concrete question about its fixture or its act.
Shared fixture logic has a named home (setUp/@BeforeEach/before/given/fixtures, or R's before-each hook) while test-specific state stays in the test body, instead of both being smeared together.
The structure transfers: the same three beats map onto xUnit classes, BDD blocks, Gherkin scenarios and table-driven cases, so the discipline survives a change of language or framework.
Drift becomes visible: a second act, or an assertion inside the arrange beat, stands out as a signal to split the test or extract a builder.

The pattern derives from command-query separation (Bertrand Meyer): the act beat is a command (side-effect-producing operation) and the assert beat is a query over its result, making the pattern's rationale explicit.
Consistent AAA structure across a test suite means developers can scan tests rapidly, reducing cognitive load during code review and debugging.
tradeoffs: The beats are a convention, not a mechanism: nothing in a compiler or runner stops act and assert from interleaving, and even macro-based DSLs such as Catch2's GIVEN/WHEN/THEN state that they do not enforce sequencing - only review or the visible markers keep the structure honest.
Shared setup moves part of the arrange beat out of the test method, so the reader must look in two places; as a fixture grows, the three-beat legibility the pattern promised quietly disappears.

One act per test rules out legitimate cumulative-state scenarios, and teams then either stuff assertions into the arrange beat or chain tests that depend on each other - both worse than the multi-step test they replaced.
A test with all three beats can still verify several behaviours at once: the pattern organises the beats, it does not produce a single-condition test, so it can make a bloated test look disciplined.
Test doubles belong to the arrange beat and are outside the pattern's control: a mock-heavy fixture can make the assert beat pass for the wrong reason without any structural violation.

The BDD vocabulary costs something - GIVEN/WHEN/THEN macros, feature files and behaviour specs add a DSL to learn and names to maintain, which is overhead wherever three comments would have carried the same information.
Assertion-only tests (no arrange needed) or action-without-return tests can make the act beat feel like a no-op; naming conventions like `result =` help but require discipline.

participants.responsibility: Establishes the preconditions of the test - the system under test, its collaborators, input values and any prior state - and does nothing else. In constructor-test variants this phase may also include creating the SUT itself.

Performs the single call or interaction whose behaviour this test verifies; it contains no assertions and no fixture work. In command-test variants the SUT is created in arrange, and act triggers the command. Exceptions triggered by the act can be captured with framework constructs (pytest.raises, assertThrows, assertThatThrownBy) and still constitute the act beat.

Checks the observable outcome - returned value, post-state, raised error or recorded interaction - and fails with a message that names the expectation. Multiple assertions are acceptable when they verify closely related aspects of the same outcome; unrelated assertions signal a missing test.

Restores the world after the test: releases files, connections, transactions and temporary state, normally through the framework's after-each hook or RAII rather than inside the test body. In the Four-Phase Test model this is a distinct fourth phase; in AAA it is typically handled implicitly.

The person the pattern serves: must be able to say, without tracing the system under test, which call is the behaviour under test and what was expected of it. The reader is the primary audience; optimize for their comprehension over the writer's convenience.

use_cases: Rewriting 'arrange, act, assert, act, assert, arrange more, act, assert' tests into one behaviour per test so that the interesting configurations become visible.
Introducing a team-wide convention - comment markers, GIVEN/WHEN/THEN blocks or a BDD runner - across a suite that is the only documentation of a legacy module.
Writing the assert beat first when working from a bug report ('suppose it worked, how would I be able to tell?'), then filling in arrange and act around the observation point.
Reading and onboarding: a suite whose tests each show one act can be walked in order to learn what the system does.
Driving acceptance specifications with non-programmers, where the Given-When-Then form of the same three beats becomes the feature file the business reviews.
Parameterising one behaviour over many inputs as a table-driven test: each row is one arrange-act-assert case and fails on its own.
Constructor tests: when the SUT is created and immediately queried (no command), the create call is both the arrange and the act. Wake calls this the constructor-test variant.
Exception tests: wrapping the act in pytest.raises/assertThrows combines the act and assert into one block, still readable as the act-and-assert beat.
Behaviour-verification tests (mock-based): the mock assertion (verify) is part of the assert beat alongside state assertions.
Exercising an ASP.NET Core controller with NUnit: arrange the request, collaborators and authorization state, invoke one action, then assert the response and one related observable side effect.
Testing a Django service or API view with pytest: use narrowly scoped fixtures for the database and user state, call the view or service once, then assert the response and persisted outcome.

Testing a Node.js module with Jest or a business-readable Cucumber scenario: arrange the dependency state, perform one command, and assert its returned payload or emitted event; use Gherkin only when the scenario itself is a shared specification.

Testing .NET code under Microsoft's unit testing best practices: keep exactly one Act per test method, and when the same behaviour must hold for several inputs, replace a second act with a parameterised theory or data-row test instead of a second act.

Writing Rails request or system specs under the Even Better Specs guidelines: each example arranges its own state inline, performs one request or UI interaction, and asserts the outcome, rather than hunting through let/subject chains.

Structuring Node.js unit tests with Jest or Mocha per the Node Best Practices AAA guide: arrange the module and its doubles, call the function under test once, assert the returned value or emitted side effect; extract long arrange blocks into named helpers so act and assert stay visible.
avoid_when: The test is a genuine end-to-end journey (log in, navigate, mutate, observe) whose honest form is one script; split it into per-behaviour tests only when every step has its own observable outcome.
A throwaway spike or REPL check: an ad-hoc script with a print or exit code is enough - do not build a test fixture around it.
The runner already imposes the structure and reports it (Gherkin scenarios, table-driven cases, property-based tests), so repeating the beats as comments only duplicates what the framework shows.
Performance, soak or timing tests, where the point is behaviour over time rather than one outcome; measure and report instead of asserting a single result.
The setup so dominates the act that the test is really a fixture story - move it to shared fixtures or a builder first, then apply the beats to what remains.

A Given-When-Then DSL such as Cucumber is already the test's executable structure; use it when business-readable scenarios and step reuse matter, and do not duplicate AAA comments in the feature or step definition.

An act-as-assert construct such as pytest.raises, assertThrows or assertThatThrownBy is the clearest check for one exception-producing call; forcing a separate result variable can obscure the expected exception boundary.
A characterization test deliberately records broad, possibly surprising existing behaviour before change; do not impose a narrow AAA expectation until the behaviour worth preserving is understood.
anti_patterns: Comment theatre: unlike a real AAA test, the // Arrange // Act // Assert markers are present but the code underneath is still one interleaved script, so labels cannot localise a failure.
A single 'test everything' method: unlike one-behaviour AAA cases, it performs several acts and assertions per entity, so one red result still requires tracing unrelated state.
Assertions inside the arrange beat: unlike an assert about the SUT outcome, a setup check turns a fixture defect into a failure that looks like a behaviour defect.
Fixture accretion: unlike a self-contained AAA arrange, everything migrates into setUp/@BeforeEach/'before' until the test body no longer says how it differs from its neighbours.
One act per test enforced mechanically: unlike a deliberate cumulative-state test, it splits a required sequence into order-dependent tests with hidden coupling.
Turning AAA into a metric: unlike a readability discipline, counting statements per beat or banning multi-assert tests produces compliant-looking tests nobody can understand.
Assert-only tests: unlike an explicit AAA case, they hide the preconditions that enable the act and make the test depend on implicit setup.
Hardcoded magic values: unlike intent-revealing arrange data, scattered literals make the fixture's business meaning opaque.
Over-mocking in arrange: unlike a state-based AAA fixture, a graph built entirely from mocks can make the assert pass for the wrong reason without any structural violation.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: precondition, interaction and expectation each have exactly one place in the test.
Single responsibility at test level: one test verifies one behaviour; extra assertions signal a missing test or a missing helper.
Fail fast with meaning: the assert beat is the only place a test may fail, so a red test maps to one behaviour.
Command-query separation as the spine of the test: the act beat is a command, the assert beat is a query over its result (Bill Wake derives the pattern from this separation).
Optimise for the reader over the writer: tests are read far more often than they are written, and the structure exists for that reader.
Single Condition Test (from xUnit Test Patterns): each test verifies exactly one test condition, giving good Defect Localization - when a test fails you know exactly what is wrong in the SUT.
Test isolation: each test builds its own Fresh Fixture to avoid Interacting Tests (erratic tests that pass or fail depending on execution order).
best_practices: Write the assert beat first when the expected outcome is clear; it fixes the observation point and any missing seam before arrange code exists. This is also the 'Assert First' technique Bill Wake attributes to Brian Marick.
Keep exactly one act per test; when a second act appears, extract the shared steps into a helper or split the test - keep a multi-step test only when the cumulative state itself is the behaviour.

Make the beats visible - a blank line plus a comment, a section/given-when-then macro or a runner step - so interleaving is easy to catch in review. Comment labels are not required but help during team onboarding.

Push only cross-test fixture work into setUp/@BeforeEach/'before'; anything one test needs differently stays in that test's arrange beat. Avoid putting mock setups in shared setup - keep them in each test's arrange beat so the fixture is self-contained.
Assert equality with expected and actual operands rather than a boolean flag, and add the message the runner cannot infer from the values.
Keep teardown off the assert path: after-each hooks, RAII/using/with or try/finally, so a failing assertion cannot skip cleanup.
When a fixture genuinely needs composing, extract a Test Data Builder or Object Mother for the arrange beat instead of letting the arrange section grow.
Use intent-revealing variable names: name the SUT 'subject' or the object type, and name the act result 'result' or 'actual' for consistency across the suite.
Name test functions to complete the sentence: 'test_[what]_[condition]_[expected outcome]'. The function name is the first clue during CI failure triage.
Limit assertions per test to 1-3 closely related checks. If assertions verify unrelated outcomes, split into separate tests.
For exception tests, wrap the act in a raises/catch block - this combines act and assert naturally and should be commented as 'Act & Assert' to show intent.
When the act has no return value, capture it with result = act() and assert result is None (or equivalent), pinning the SUT's behaviour and making it clear the act completed without error.
Use pytest.mark.parametrize for covering many inputs of the same behaviour - each parametrised row is a complete AAA case.

Avoid let/background/fixture lazy-loading for test-specific setup that the test reader needs to understand; inline arrange with a clear blank-line separation is more readable than hunting for implicitly-loaded fixtures.
pitfalls: Ritual beats: comments are present but the code is still interleaved - the labels describe a structure that is not there.
Fixture accretion: everything moves into setUp/@BeforeEach until the test body loses its distinctiveness.
Assertions in the arrange beat: turning fixture defects into apparent behaviour failures.
Boolean-only assertions: assert is_valid() hides the actual value; assertEqual(expected, actual) gives a useful failure message.
Multiple acts in one test without separation: a failure cannot be localised without manual investigation.
Over-mocking: a mock-heavy arrange makes the assert pass for the wrong reason - state-based assertions are generally more robust than mock verification alone.
Hardcoded magic values in arrange without explanatory variables, obscuring fixture intent.
Order-dependent tests created when one act per test is enforced mechanically on genuinely cumulative-state scenarios.
Comments or section markers used as a metric rather than a discipline - tests become compliant but still unreadable.
Shared setup with implicit dependencies: tests that work only because an earlier test left state behind.
Tests that assert too many unrelated outcomes, violating single-condition test principle and making failure diagnosis ambiguous.
Long arrange sections (>10 lines) that bury the test's purpose; extract into fixtures or builders when this happens.

Wrong move -> how it fails -> instead: put every dependency and default into beforeEach or a fixture helper -> a fixture-god setup hides why this case passes and unrelated changes break many tests -> keep test-specific state inline and extract only named, stable builders.

Wrong move -> how it fails -> instead: append a second act after the first assertion -> a later failure cannot identify which transition broke and the test becomes state-order dependent -> split the cases, or retain the sequence only when cumulative state is the behaviour under test.

Wrong move -> how it fails -> instead: paste AAA comments around a Given-When-Then DSL or write assert(sut.act()) -> duplicated markers and a merged act/assert expression hide the boundary and weaken failure diagnostics -> use the native DSL once, or store the act result before asserting it.

Wrong move -> how it fails -> instead: enforce one-assert-per-test as a hard rule -> near-identical arrange blocks are duplicated across a dozen tests and the behaviour that distinguishes each one drowns in boilerplate -> assert everything that describes the single observable outcome and split only when assertions cover different behaviours.

Wrong move -> how it fails -> instead: mirror the implementation in the assert beat, checking internal calls and every code path -> change-detector tests pass while the behaviour breaks and fail on every refactor -> assert the externally observable outcome of one behaviour so the test survives internal restructuring.

Wrong move -> how it fails -> instead: build the fixture while simultaneously invoking the SUT, blurring arrange and act -> the reader cannot tell which call is the behaviour under test and a fixture-creation error reads like a product bug -> keep act as its own statement or section, with SUT construction in arrange (or deliberately as the constructor-test variant).

https://xp123.com/3a-arrange-act-assert/
Bill Wake. AAA and the Object Lifecycle. (2026) — Covers the constructor-test variant vs command-test variant of AAA and how they relate to the object lifecycle (create, command*, query+).
https://xp123.com/aaa-and-the-object-lifecycle/

Gerard Meszaros. xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code. (Addison-Wesley; 2007; 978-0131495050) — Chapter 19, Four-Phase Test (p. 358): fixture setup, exercise SUT, result verification, fixture teardown. The authoritative xUnit reference. Chapter 8 covers Transient Fixture Management strategies (inline, delegated, implicit setup).

Martin Fowler. GivenWhenThen. (2013) — Describes Given-When-Then as a reformulation of Meszaros' Four-Phase Test, created by Dan North and Chris Matts. BDD as BDD practitioners believe it should be done.
https://martinfowler.com/bliki/GivenWhenThen.html

Daniel Terhorst-North (Dan North). Introducing BDD. (2006) — Dan North's original BDD introduction describing how Given-When-Then was created to give TDD a better vocabulary for behaviour specification.
https://dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/

Chris Matts. Given When Then – A Cynefin Case Study. (2014) — Chris Matts recounts the literal day Given-When-Then was created (August 23, 2004) and the Cynefin framework context. Originally proposed by Matts as part of BDD with Dan North and Liz Keogh.
https://theitriskmanager.com/2014/08/08/given-when-then-a-cynefin-case-study/
Gojko Adzic. Given-When-Then. (2025) — History of Given-When-Then: proposed by Chris Matts in 2004, adopted by JBehave, RSpec, then Cucumber (2009) which popularised it as the Gherkin format.
https://www.votito.com/methods/given-when-then/

Kent Beck. Test-Driven Development: By Example. (Addison-Wesley; 2002; 978-0321146533) — Page 97 mentions the Arrange-Act-Assert structure. The book that brought TDD to a wide audience and helped canonicalise the AAA pattern.

Thoughtbot. The Arrange/Act/Assert Pattern. (2025) — Practical guide on distinguishing AAA from let/before fixture patterns; argues inline arrange with clear separation is more readable than lazy-loaded fixtures scattered across a describe block.
https://thoughtbot.com/blog/the-arrange-act-assert-pattern

James Cooke. Arrange Act Assert pattern for Python developers. (2017) — Python-specific AAA guide covering naming conventions (result = for act), fixture extraction signals, and docstring style guidance.
https://jamescooke.info/arrange-act-assert-pattern-for-python-developers.html

Anthony Sciamanna. Follow Consistent Test Patterns. (2016) — Covers the relationship between xUnit setUp and arrange; recommends keeping only object/dependency creation in setUp, not mock setup, to preserve test self-containment.
https://anthonysciamanna.com/2016/04/24/follow-consistent-test-patterns.html

React TDD. Understanding Arrange-Act-Assert. (2020) — Covers the Act-Act-Assert anti-pattern and test dependency problems; explains why splitting multi-act tests is essential for failure localisation.
https://reacttdd.com/arrange-act-assert/
Gerard Meszaros. xUnit Test Patterns (website). (2007) — Online version of Four-Phase Test pattern. Describes inline vs implicit setup/teardown strategies and when each is appropriate.
http://xunitpatterns.com/Four%20Phase%20Test.html
Martin Fowler. Specification By Example. (2004) — Foundational concept linking examples (tests) to specifications; AAA tests as a form of living specification.
https://martinfowler.com/bliki/SpecificationByExample.html

JUnit Team. Annotations. (2026) — JUnit Jupiter documents @Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach and @Nested, showing how lifecycle hooks and test methods provide the fixture and behavior boundaries around assertions.
https://docs.junit.org/6.1.3/writing-tests/annotations.html

Cucumber Team. Reference. (2026) — Gherkin defines Given as initial context, When as an event or action, and Then as an observable outcome, and warns that examples with too many steps lose expressive power as a specification.
https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference

pytest Development Team. How to use fixtures. (2026) — pytest fixtures are requested as test-function arguments, can be composed, and normally provide each test with a fresh result; this makes fixture scope part of the arrange boundary.
https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/fixtures.html
NUnit Team. Assertions. (2026) — NUnit documents the Assert.That constraint model, assertion failure behavior, and the tradeoff between one assertion per test and deliberate grouped checks.
https://docs.nunit.org/articles/nunit/writing-tests/assertions/assertions.html
Jest Team. Setup and Teardown. (2026) — Jest's beforeEach/afterEach hooks and describe scoping show how shared fixture lifecycle can support AAA while remaining visible outside the test body.
https://jestjs.io/docs/setup-teardown

Justin Toniazzo. The Arrange/Act/Assert pattern. (2025) — A community treatment contrasts inline AAA with let/before setup: hidden or over-arranged fixtures make preconditions and the act harder to find even when the test technically passes.
https://thoughtbot.com/blog/the-arrange-act-assert-pattern

Microsoft Learn. Unit testing best practices with .NET. (2025) — Official .NET guidance: keep Arrange, Act and Assert visually separated for readability and limit each test to a single Act, using separate tests or parameterised theories when more inputs are needed.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/unit-testing-best-practices

Microsoft Learn. Razor Pages unit tests in ASP.NET Core. (2025) — Official ASP.NET Core tutorial organising PageModel tests with Arrange/Act/Assert: the arrange seeds an in-memory database, the act invokes one page handler, the assert checks the result.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/test/razor-pages-tests?view=aspnetcore-9.0

Yoni Goldberg. AAA - Arrange, Act, Assert (Node Best Practices). (2024) — Node.js community best practice for AAA: keep the pattern simple and inline, and extract a long arrange into a named helper so the act and assert remain the visible core of the test.
https://github.com/goldbergyoni/nodebestpractices/blob/master/sections/testingandquality/aaa.md

Even Better Specs contributors. Even Better Specs: Guidelines for Maintainable Tests. (2025) — Rails/RSpec guidelines endorsing the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern in self-contained tests: explicit arrange in the example, request specs over controller specs, and resistance to hidden let/before fixture chains.
https://evenbetterspecs.github.io/

Manning Books (Medium). Making Better Unit Tests, Part 1: The AAA Pattern. (2019) — Critique of the rigid reading of AAA: a unit test targets a unit of behaviour, not a fixed assertion count; multiple assertions on one outcome are fine, while multiple acts signal the test has outgrown its unit.
https://manningbooks.medium.com/making-better-unit-tests-part-1-the-aaa-pattern-e016775ea6c6

related_patterns_notes.test-data-builder: Unlike Arrange-Act-Assert itself, a Test Data Builder is a fixture-construction aid: it extracts complex arrange logic into composable, intent-revealing steps without changing the test's act or assert boundary.
related_patterns_notes.object-mother: Unlike a Test Data Builder's incremental configuration, an Object Mother returns a ready-made common fixture; it keeps repeated arrange values out of AAA tests but can hide variation when overused.
related_patterns_notes.page-object: Unlike AAA, a Page Object encapsulates browser locators and interactions behind intent-revealing methods; it keeps a UI test's act to one user-goal call rather than a chain of low-level clicks.
related_patterns_notes.characterization-test: Unlike an ordinary AAA behavior test, a Characterization Test captures what the system already does (including accidental behavior) before refactoring; AAA supplies the readable observation boundary.
related_patterns_notes.humble-object: Unlike AAA's test-body structure, a Humble Object moves hard-to-test I/O behind a thin boundary so the remaining logic can be exercised with a small arrange-act-assert test.
related_patterns_notes.recording-fake: Unlike a state-only assertion, a Recording Fake stores interactions for later inspection; configuring it is arrange work, while asserting its recorded calls remains the AAA assert phase.
related_patterns_notes.given-when-then: given-when-then — Unlike AAA's code-structure convention, Given-When-Then is a behaviour-specification vocabulary: Given maps to Arrange, When to Act and Then to Assert, often with a DSL or feature file for shared domain language.
related_patterns_notes.four-phase-test: Unlike AAA's usual implicit cleanup, Four-Phase Test names fixture teardown as a fourth phase; it is the fuller xUnit Test Patterns model when resources need explicit lifecycle handling.
